ev.isl_fc_aqiqa.sheep.ok: The meat went to the neighbours, to the poor at the mosque and to the family — a third to each, as is the custom. The whole quarter knew a child had been born to you and wished you long life.
ev.isl_fc_aqiqa.silver: Only the silver for the hair
ev.isl_fc_aqiqa.silver.ok: Your hair was weighed on a jeweller's tiny scales, and your father carried a handful of silver coins to the poor — more than the weight required.
ev.isl_fc_aqiqa.later.ok: "The aqiqa can wait — God is in no hurry," your father decided. The silver for the hair was given away, and he promised the ram as soon as business picked up.
ev.isl_fc_aqiqa.title: The aqiqa
ev.isl_fc_aqiqa.text: As soon as you were born, your father whispered the call to prayer into your right ear, so that the first word you heard would be the name of God. On the seventh day you will be named, your head will be shaved, and its weight in silver given to the poor. Custom also calls for slaughtering {g:two rams|a ram} to feed the neighbours and the needy — the aqiqa. But mutton is dear this year.
ev.isl_fc_aqiqa.note: According to the hadith, the call to prayer is whispered into a newborn's ear, and on the seventh day the child is named, its head shaved, silver given away to the weight of the hair, and a sacrifice made — the aqiqa. Most jurists prescribed two rams for a boy and one for a girl; the Malikis, as in al-Andalus, one for each. If means were lacking, the aqiqa could be held later.
ev.isl_fc_aqiqa_guest.title: Meat from your aqiqa
ev.isl_fc_aqiqa_guest.text: A shopkeeper in the bazaar stopped you and looked you over for a long time. "When you were born, I was a hungry boy at the mosque gate and ate meat from your aqiqa," he said. "Now I have a shop of my own. Take this — for that dinner." And he pressed a length of good cloth into your hands.
ev.isl_fc_aqiqa_late.title: A late aqiqa
ev.isl_fc_aqiqa_late.text: At last your father's business has turned up, and he kept his word: he bought a ram at the market and invited the neighbours to your aqiqa — even though you are already running about the yard and helping carry the dishes yourself. They seated you in the place of honour, and you feel like the most important person in the street.
ev.isl_fc_qirad.caravan: Give it to a merchant under mudaraba
ev.isl_fc_qirad.caravan.ok: A scribe drew up the contract, witnesses set their seals, and the money left with a caravan across the desert. Your father put the scroll away in the chest: "That is {g:his|her} share."
ev.isl_fc_qirad.shop: Buy a share in a shop
ev.isl_fc_qirad.shop.ok: A quarter of a coppersmith's shop by the bazaar gate was bought in your name. A few coins come from it every month and are put aside in a purse of their own.
ev.isl_fc_qirad.keep.ok: "Let the money stay at home — it's safer," your father decided. What a baby needs, after all, is milk, not a contract.
ev.isl_fc_qirad.title: A share in your name
ev.isl_fc_qirad.text: To mark your birth your father wants to set money aside in your name. He could hand it to a merchant he knows who is leaving with a caravan, under a mudaraba contract: the merchant trades, the profit is shared, and any loss, should disaster strike, falls on you. He could buy you a share in a shop in the bazaar — a modest income, but a sure one. Or he could leave the money alone.
ev.isl_fc_qirad.note: Mudaraba (in the western Islamic lands, qirad) was a partnership in which one party supplied the money and the other traded with it; profit was shared by agreement, and losses fell on the owner of the money. Muslims, Christians and Jews all traded this way: hundreds of such deals survive in the documents of the Cairo Geniza.
ev.isl_fc_qirad_return.trust.ok: You took the money and thanked him. The merchant left pleased — perhaps a little too pleased.
ev.isl_fc_qirad_return.audit.success: You spent two evenings over his entries and found where he had "forgotten" half the profit. The merchant went red and paid in full.
ev.isl_fc_qirad_return.audit.failure: You could make nothing of his figures and only angered him. He counted out less than he had promised and left, slamming the door.
ev.isl_fc_qirad_return.title: The merchant returns
ev.isl_fc_qirad_return.text: The merchant who was once entrusted with money in your name has come back from distant lands, older and sunburnt. He opened his account book: the caravans crossed the desert and back, there were losses and there was profit, and your share — here it is, in a little bag. You can take his word for it, or sit down and check the entries.
ev.isl_fc_qirad_shop.title: A quarter of a shop
ev.isl_fc_qirad_shop.text: The coppersmith in whose shop you have owned a quarter share since infancy called you in and laid out on the counter everything that had built up over the years, coin by coin. "You're grown now — this is yours." He also showed you how the takings are reckoned — that will come in handy.
